title: TFSA vs RRSP: Which Should You Open First? (Canada)
description: TFSA vs RRSP for Canadian beginners: how each is taxed, the 2026 limits, what the RRSP deduction is really worth at your income, and which comes first.
keywords: tfsa vs rrsp which first tfsa limit 2026 rrsp limit 2026 canada beginners
takeaways: On a lower income, the TFSA usually comes first. The RRSP gets better as your income rises.
For 2026, new TFSA room is $7,000 and the RRSP limit is 18% of last year's earned income, up to $33,810.
TFSA withdrawals are tax-free and the room comes back next year. RRSP withdrawals are taxed.
body:
If you have started reading about saving money in Canada, two accounts show up everywhere: the TFSA and the RRSP. Most people know both are supposed to be good. Far fewer know which one to open first, and the answer depends mostly on how much you earn.

To be clear up front: this article is about Canada only. The TFSA and the RRSP are Canadian accounts, the dollar figures are the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) limits for 2026, and none of these rules apply in the US or anywhere else.

The short version: if you earn under roughly $55,000 a year, the TFSA usually comes first. The RRSP gets more attractive as your income climbs. Here is the reasoning, with the actual 2026 numbers and one worked example, so you can check the logic yourself.

## The short answer

- Earn under about $55,000: open a TFSA first and put your early savings there.
- Your job matches RRSP contributions: get the full match first, then go back to the TFSA. A match is extra pay.
- Earn well above $55,000 and expect a lower income in retirement: the RRSP starts to pull ahead, because your deduction is worth more today than the tax you will pay on withdrawal.
- Given enough money, most people end up using both. The order matters most early on, when you can only fund one at a time.

## What a TFSA is, in plain terms

The TFSA (Tax-Free Savings Account) is badly named. It sounds like a plain savings account, but it is really a tax shelter that can hold cash, GICs, mutual funds, ETFs, and individual stocks.

You contribute money you have already paid income tax on. From that point on, the CRA leaves it alone. Interest, dividends, and growth inside the account are never taxed, and neither is anything you withdraw.

### How much you can put in

For 2026, the CRA set new TFSA room at $7,000. Room starts building in the year you turn 18, as long as you are a resident of Canada with a Social Insurance Number, and unused room carries forward. If you were already 18 when the TFSA launched in 2009 and have never contributed, your total room in 2026 adds up to $109,000.

Your personal number is probably much smaller than that, so check it in CRA My Account before you contribute. Keep your own record too, because the CRA figure can lag behind recent deposits.

New to investing itself? Read [how to start investing with little money](/blog/start-investing-with-little-money/) once the account is open.

### Taking money out

This is where the TFSA earns its keep. You can withdraw any amount, at any time, for any reason, and pay no tax on it. The one catch is timing: the amount you take out is only added back to your contribution room on January 1 of the following year. Put the money back in the same calendar year, without other spare room, and you have over-contributed. The CRA taxes an excess TFSA amount at 1% for each month it stays in the account.

TFSA withdrawals also do not count as income, so they do not reduce income-tested federal benefits such as Old Age Security later in life.

## What an RRSP is, in plain terms

The RRSP (Registered Retirement Savings Plan) works the other way around. Money you contribute can be deducted from your taxable income, so you pay less tax now. The tax bill is not gone, just postponed. When you take money out, the withdrawal is added to your income and taxed in that year.

### How much you can put in

Your new RRSP room each year is 18% of the earned income you reported the year before, up to a dollar cap set by the CRA: $33,810 for 2026. On a $40,000 salary, 18% is $7,200 of new room, well under the cap. Unused room carries forward, a workplace pension reduces your new room, and your exact limit is printed on your notice of assessment after you file your taxes.

### Two rules people miss

First, you do not have to claim the deduction in the year you contribute. You can put money in now and save the deduction for a later year, when your income and your tax rate are higher. For people early in their working lives, that flexibility matters a lot, and the worked example below shows why.

Second, withdrawals are a one-way door. Money taken out of an RRSP is taxed as income, and the contribution room is gone for good. There are two narrow exceptions, the Home Buyers' Plan and the Lifelong Learning Plan, which let you borrow from your RRSP for a first home or for schooling. Outside those two plans, treat RRSP money as money you will not touch until retirement. One hard end date: by December 31 of the year you turn 71, an RRSP has to be closed or converted, usually into a RRIF.

## TFSA vs RRSP, side by side

|                                  | TFSA                                | RRSP                                        |
|----------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| Tax break when you contribute    | None, after-tax money                   | Deductible from your taxable income             |
| Tax while the money grows        | None                                    | None, tax deferred until withdrawal             |
| Tax when you withdraw            | None, ever                              | Withdrawal is taxed as income                   |
| New room in 2026                 | $7,000, the same for everyone eligible | 18% of your 2025 earned income, up to $33,810  |
| How room builds                  | From the year you turn 18               | From earned income on your tax return           |
| Do withdrawals restore room?     | Yes, on January 1 of the next year      | No, gone for good (two borrowing plans aside)   |
| Effect on income-tested benefits | Withdrawals are not income, no effect   | Withdrawals count as income                     |
| Deadline to use it               | None, you can keep a TFSA for life      | Close or convert by end of the year you turn 71 |
| Usually best for                 | Lower incomes and flexible goals        | Higher incomes, retirement savings              |

## The $40,000 example: what the deduction is really worth

Here is the part most comparison articles skip. An RRSP deduction is not worth a fixed amount. It is worth whatever tax rate applies to the income it removes, and at a low income that rate is small.

Illustration, with made-up numbers: you earn a $40,000 salary in Ontario and have $3,000 to save. The rates are the real 2026 federal and Ontario rates published by the CRA, ignoring other credits and deductions to keep the math clean.

### Option A: claim the $3,000 deduction now

At a $40,000 income, every dollar of that deduction comes out of the lowest brackets. Federally, the first $58,523 of taxable income is taxed at 14% in 2026, so the deduction saves $420 on $3,000. In Ontario, the lowest rate is 5.05% on the first $53,891, worth another $151.50. Total value of the deduction today: $571.50.

### Option B: claim the same deduction in a $90,000 year

Say your income rises to $90,000 in a few years and you claim the same $3,000 deduction then. Those dollars come off income taxed at 20.5% federally and 9.15% in Ontario, so the deduction is worth $615 plus $274.50: $889.50 in total. Same contribution, $318 more in tax saved, just for claiming it in a higher-income year.

|                                  | Claimed at $40,000 income | Claimed at $90,000 income |
|----------------------------------|--------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Federal tax saved                | 14% of $3,000 = $420         | 20.5% of $3,000 = $615       |
| Ontario tax saved                | 5.05% of $3,000 = $151.50    | 9.15% of $3,000 = $274.50    |
| **Total value of the deduction** | **$571.50**                   | **$889.50**                   |

### What the TFSA does with the same $3,000

The $3,000 in a TFSA gets you no deduction at all. In exchange, it is never taxed again: not the growth, not the withdrawal. At a $40,000 income, giving up a deduction worth $571.50 for that deal is usually a good trade. At a much higher income, the trade flips, which is why the RRSP matters more later in your career.

When RRSP money comes out in retirement, it is taxed at whatever rate applies then. A lower rate than today means you come out ahead. The same rate or higher means the TFSA was the better home for the money. Since nobody knows their retirement rate for certain, the flexible account makes sense as a first step.

Rates differ by province, so your exact numbers will move around. The ranking of the two accounts does not.

## So which one should you open first?

### If you earn under about $55,000

Start with the TFSA. While your income sits in the lowest federal bracket, which runs up to $58,523 of taxable income in 2026, an RRSP deduction saves you the least it ever will. The TFSA also pulls double duty while you are getting started, since it can hold the emergency savings you are building at the same time. If that fund is still small, [how to build an emergency fund on a small income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/) is a good companion read.

### If your employer matches RRSP contributions

Take the match first, before this whole debate. If your employer adds money when you contribute, that is part of your pay, and leaving it unclaimed costs more than this whole choice ever will. Contribute enough to get the full match, then send your next dollars to the TFSA.

### If you earn more, or a big raise is close

Once your income is well into the higher brackets, the RRSP case gets strong: deduct at a high rate now, withdraw at a lower rate in retirement. A common pattern is to fill the TFSA first anyway, for flexibility, then move to the RRSP, then put the RRSP tax refund into the TFSA so the same dollars work twice. If a first home is on your list, it is also worth reading up on the First Home Savings Account (FHSA) before you decide, since it was built for that goal. For the saving itself, see [how to save for a house deposit on a low income](/blog/save-for-house-deposit-low-income/).

And if you are still sorting out where your money goes each month, start even simpler: [how to budget on less than $1,000 a month](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/) covers the basics, and [how to set financial goals you actually reach](/blog/set-financial-goals/) can help you decide what this first account is actually for.

## Mistakes that cost people money

- Over-contributing to a TFSA. The 1% monthly tax on excess amounts adds up quickly. Check your room before a deposit, not after.
- Putting a withdrawal back too soon. Room from a TFSA withdrawal only returns on January 1 of the next year, and recontributing early is the most common way people over-contribute by accident.
- Spending the RRSP refund. Part of the RRSP's advantage lives in that refund. Spend it instead of saving it, and some of the advantage goes with it.
- Raiding the RRSP early. A withdrawal outside the Home Buyers' Plan or Lifelong Learning Plan is taxed as income, and the room never comes back.
- Waiting for the perfect answer. Either account beats leaving savings in a regular taxable account. Opening the less-than-perfect one is a small mistake. Sitting in cash for years while you decide is a bigger one.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I have a TFSA and an RRSP at the same time?

Yes, and most people eventually do. They are separate accounts with separate room, and contributing to one does not reduce the other.

### I am a student with a part-time job. Does an RRSP make sense yet?

Probably not as your first move. Part-time income usually sits in the lowest tax bracket, so a deduction is worth very little. A TFSA gives you tax-free growth with full flexibility, and your RRSP room keeps building in the background for when your income is higher.

### I just moved to Canada. Which account should I open?

Both accounts are tied to your Social Insurance Number and your life in Canada. TFSA room starts in the year you become a resident of Canada for tax purposes. RRSP room builds from Canadian earned income you report on a tax return, so in your first year here you may have little or no RRSP room yet. For most newcomers, the TFSA is the practical place to start.

### What if I need my TFSA money for a car repair?

That is exactly the kind of thing it is good at. Withdraw what you need, pay no tax, and the room comes back on the following January 1. Just do not put the money back in the same year unless you have other unused room.

### Does it matter where I open the account?

Banks, credit unions, and online brokerages all offer both. Compare account fees and transfer fees before you choose. And remember that CRA limits apply to you as a person, across every TFSA or RRSP you hold combined, not per account.

## A quick note before you decide

This article is general information about Canadian accounts, not personal financial or tax advice. CRA limits and tax rates change over time, and provincial rates differ from the Ontario figures used in the example. Check your own contribution room with the CRA before a large contribution, and consider speaking with a qualified tax professional.
